documents: Avagyan et al. 2022, Geology and palaeoenvironment of Karin Tak Cave (Lesser Caucasus), Journal of Cave and Karst Studies 84(1):14-26 (published PDF)

entry.evidence: The principal aims of this paper are therefore to: (i) describe the formation of Karin Tak cave in terms of geological processes

sequences.source_document: Avagyan et al. 2022, Journal of Cave and Karst Studies 84(1):14-26

steps.action: Set three aims: explain cave formation, map the depth and extent of soft floor sediments by geophysics to guide excavation, and reconstruct the palaeoenvironment from floor sediments.
steps.quote: The principal aims of this paper are therefore to: (i) describe the formation of Karin Tak cave in terms of geological processes

steps.action: Proposed, from cited regional Neogene uplift and Sarmatian regression, that karstification and cave initiation began in the Neogene.
steps.quote: We suggest that the development of the Karin Tak was initiated during this period.

steps.action: Mapped cave structure: orientation parallel to regional fractures, fracture-guided oval vertical shafts, surface sinkholes, and a left-lateral strike-slip fault at the entrance.
steps.quote: indicate intense circulation of meteoric groundwater with the leeching and dissolution of the limestone host rock

steps.action: Inferred that fault reactivation opened meteoric-water routes and controlled cave development.
steps.quote: Reactivation of faults and the opening of subsurface migration routes for meteoric waters had an important role in development of the cave.

steps.action: Ran 2D and 3D ground-penetrating radar surveys (400 MHz) in the central chamber, sliced into 0.25 m depth sections and built a 3D model of blocks and soft sediment.
steps.quote: The ground-penetrating radar allowed qualitative and quantitative surveys of the cave floor deposits.

steps.action: Interpreted the buried GPR blocks and boulders as debris from roof collapse.
steps.quote: The GPR surveys reveal the presence of buried limestone blocks and boulders, which are the possible result of cave roof collapse.

steps.action: Placed the excavation pit where GPR showed fewer blocks and boulders.
steps.quote: The location of the pit was chosen according to GPR survey as a place with fewer blocks and boulders.

steps.action: Ground-truthed the GPR interpretation against the blocks exposed in the pit sections.
steps.quote: [...] pit sections through the cave sediment.

steps.action: Logged six stratigraphic layers on the SE and SW pit walls by particle size, texture, fabric and Munsell colour.
steps.quote: Sedimentological investigations of the southeast and southwest walls of the pit (Fig. 3), which was excavated in 2016-2018, showed six stratigraphic layers

steps.action: Took 14C ages for layers A and B on bones from Antonosyan et al. (2019).
steps.quote: The layers A and B were formed between 24,589 ± 149 BP and 22,947 ± 204 BP

steps.action: Classified sediments into autochthonous collapse breccia, attributed mostly to seismically triggered collapse, and allochthonous washed-in, detrital, biological and chemical deposits.
steps.quote: Breakdown products consist of fragments of bedrock with a range of clast sizes, most of which result from cave collapse due to seismic activity.

steps.action: Determined light and heavy mineral fractions of layers A-D by the immersion method, with carbonate content.
steps.quote: The heavy mineral assemblages are characterized by clear predominance of opaque minerals with abundant ilmenite

steps.action: Counted more than 400 palynomorphs per sample from the pit walls and identified pollen taxa per layer; preservation was poor.
steps.quote: More than 400 grains were counted for each sample, and grain proportions were calculated based on the sum of all palynomorphs present.

steps.action: Measured trace elements in nine pit sediment samples by portable XRF and compared the profiles between layers, notably adjacent layers F and G.
steps.quote: Results showed comparable high contents of Pb, Cr, Rb, Ba, Fe, Mo, Co, Ti, As, Zn, Zr, V, and Mn in layer F

steps.action: Checked XRF accuracy and precision against NIST standard reference materials, a SiO2 blank and lab duplicates (Methods).
steps.quote: QA/QC showed that the accuracy and precision of the analyses were 2.2−15.4 % and 0.1−6.9 %, respectively.

steps.action: Compared the XRF composition of a nearby chert lens with layer F and found similar elemental ratios.
steps.quote: some elemental ratios are similar to those in layer F

steps.action: Set an epigenic origin, indicated by shafts, sinkholes and speleothems, against an early hypogenic influence suggested by cupolas, as at Azokh Cave.
steps.quote: the hypogenic influence is not excluded as in the case of Azokh Cave

steps.action: Weighed the morphological evidence and judged epigenic processes dominant, with any hypogenic part minimal.
steps.quote: Even if there were hypogenic parts in the formation of the cave, it is minimal and epigenetic ones are dominant.

steps.action: Inferred a moist, cool temperate climate from the conifer-dominated pollen profile, and long transport from inertinite.
steps.quote: The overall pollen profile is dominated by trees that are adapted to relatively moist and cool temperate areas

steps.action: Checked the pollen-based reconstruction against the independent aDNA faunal record of Antonosyan et al. (2019) and found it consistent: no dramatic LGM change.
steps.quote: The new pollen data presented in this study is consistent with the results of Antonosyan et al. (2019)

steps.action: Attributed the positive As, Cr, Cu, Pb, Zn and Ba anomalies in layer F to skeletal and organic detritus or charcoal, and Fe and Ti to bones or ilmenite.
steps.quote: As, Cr, Cu, Pb, Zn, and Ba positive anomalies can be result of concentrations of skeletal and organic detritus or charcoals

steps.action: Excluded metallurgy as the source of the Cu, Zn and Mo enrichment because the layers predate the Copper and Bronze Ages.
steps.quote: they are not related to human activity such as metallurgy, because the age of the layers (>41,700 BP)

steps.action: Proposed that the chert, a probable tool of unknown stratigraphic position, was a hominin raw material, and called for more finds.
steps.quote: The aforementioned data shows the high probability of using the chert as a raw material, but more finds will be needed

steps.action: Concluded: tectonically controlled, mainly epigenic cave; three-stage development model (Fig. 14); two collapses of presumed seismic origin; non-dramatic LGM climate and a possible refugium; layer F indicates hominin activity.
steps.quote: The pollen record evidence of non-dramatic climate change during LGM MIS 2 in the area

tree.answer: Karst cave formation and Late Pleistocene floor-sediment record at a hominin site
No; past processes known only from structures, sediments, pollen and geochemistry
Describe cave genesis, map soft sediments for excavation, reconstruct the palaeoenvironment
Epigenic vs hypogenic origin; metallurgy vs natural or organic sources of metal enrichment
Weakly: shafts, sinkholes and speleothems vs cupolas; layer age vs metallurgy
Found, not set: one cave, one pit section
Partly: GPR ground-truthed in the pit; pollen consistent with cited aDNA; XRF QA/QC
Epigenic origin dominant; cold temperate climate with non-dramatic LGM change, kept as best explanation

end.claim: Pollen from the Karin Tak cave-floor sediments, dominated by conifers with Fraxinus and Quercus, indicates a cold temperate continental Late Pleistocene climate with no dramatic change during the LGM, consistent with a refugium favourable to hominins.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the palynological counts from the pit-wall layers there would be no palaeoenvironmental claim; the geochemistry and mineralogy only qualify it.

gates.evidence: The work is descriptive and aim-driven: structural mapping, GPR, a pit and lab analyses; no stated hypothesis directed the acquisition (GPR chose the pit location only to avoid blocks, p. 18). The pollen reconstruction could have disagreed with the cited aDNA record but did not (p. 24); the epigenic claim rests on morphological indicators, with hypogenic influence explicitly not excluded (p. 23). Nothing was fixed before the data.

imports.item: Ancient DNA faunal identifications and genetic continuity results used as context and as an independent comparison for the pollen reconstruction
EPA Method 6200 portable XRF protocol, ISO-11464 sample preparation, NIST standard reference materials
Interpretation of chert as a hominin lithic raw material and of layers as evidence of hominin activity

limits: Headline palaeoclimate claim: best_explanation, based on pollen from few layers with poor preservation and no species-level resolution (p. 22); ages are cited from Antonosyan et al. (2019), not measured here, and the stated age ranges differ (24,589-22,947 BP on p. 20 vs 24.803-34.486 cal BP on p. 24). Sub-claims: tectonic, mainly epigenic origin, best_explanation (hypogenic not excluded, p. 23); Neogene initiation, best_explanation inferred from regional cited tectonics without direct dating (p. 16); two collapses of 'presumed seismic origin', best_explanation with no seismic test (p. 25); GPR map of blocks vs soft sediment, ground-truthed only qualitatively (p. 18); layer F hominin activity and chert raw material, weak, with one chert piece of unknown stratigraphic position (p. 24). The XRF interpretation carries an unresolved caveat on post-depositional contamination (p. 24). Only one pit, with nine XRF samples and no replicate pits. The acknowledgments mention anonymous reviewers who improved the first version (p. 25), but no review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded. The steps follow the document's order; the actual chronology of fieldwork (pit 2016-2018) relative to the GPR is not fully stated, and that the GPR preceded the pit is an inference from p. 18.
